MADAYANTIKĀ: Be gracious, O Blessed One! Save the illustrious one who has compassion for those in distress—Madayantika, whose life is now in doubt because of him. (1) THE OTHERS: Alas, woe! What must we witness now?
MADAYANTIKĀ: Oh, how wonderful! Makaranda, that full moon, has now awakened.
(*Ammahe* expresses joy and wonder. MĀLATĪ: Congratulations on your good fortune! Indeed, I was saying that your dear friend Makaranda has truly awakened. (2)
"By good fortune! By joy! May you prosper!"—this is the manner of speaking when requesting a congratulatory blessing (*vardhāpana*).
"Smelling the head" (*śirovaghrāṇa*) is the traditional practice of the elders for the sake of increasing longevity. "The others [say]: 'What is pleasing has come to pass for us.'"
Buddharakṣitā: Friend Madayantikā, this is indeed he.
(The word *halā* is an address to a female friend.
Madayantikā: I already knew that this was Mādhava, and that this person was also he.
The explicit mention of Makaranda’s name by his own name indicates the intention of accepting him as her husband. BUDDHARAKṢITĀ: "Am I a speaker of truth?
[She asks] this in the sense of seeking confirmation.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Indeed, those like you do not show partiality toward such as these. Furthermore, the report of Mālatī’s affection for this noble-souled one is most delightful.
[KĀMANDAKĪ]: "Delightful" means captivating, because it has come about without effort. "Exalted" means surpassing, because it arose preceded by assistance, such as the slaying of the tiger.

[Makaranda: *Avaskanda* means a sudden assault or crushing defeat. *Abhijātā* refers to one belonging to a noble family. Her identity is generally known through the association of her physical appearance, dress, attendants, and so forth. *Abhyupapatti* means assistance or favor.
The *vimarṣa* (perplexity or conflict) of the two heroes arises from the apprehension that they might cause mutual distress.

Madayantikā: Friend Mālatī, you have indeed been my dear friend and sister to me ever since we lived in the same city and played together in the dust; now, moreover, you have become the very ornament of my home.
TATHĀ—By the grace of your blessing. Friend Lavaṅgikā, our desires have been fulfilled by your arrival. "Fulfilled" means satisfied. LAVAṄGIKĀ—Friend, this must be discussed among us as well.

"Regarding what you have deliberated—that 'our desires will be fulfilled by the acquisition of you'—we too say this very thing. By that, it is said cryptically: 'Our own desires will be fulfilled when you are married to Makaranda. But openly, it means: 'By the acquisition of you, our royal friends, we, the king's servants, shall indeed have our desires fulfilled. Or else, these very words of yours are precisely what we must deliberate upon."

In our view, however, this is the interpretation: "By this very [means], your desires have been fulfilled. And this has also been stated by way of *śleṣa* (double entendre): "We possess in this matter a substance in the form of a minister named Kāmandakī; therefore, this [plan] is thwarted.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Buddhārakṣitā, let us now celebrate the great festival of the wedding. BUDDHĀRAKṢITĀ: Friend, let us go.

Lavaṅgikā: Blessed One, from the way the spreading movements of Madayantikā and Makaranda’s glances—which are as beautiful as a wreath of blooming blue lotuses, charming in their steady yet trembling edges, and lovely with a lingering wonder and joy held deep within their hearts—revolve, I conjecture that these two have attained the fulfillment of their desires through their union.

In the heart, during nourishment—that is, in satiety—those two wonders and joys which overflow—that is, do not find room—having made them beautiful by means of those two, they are swayed—that is, turned askance—and steadfast—that is, long-enduring—and captivating at the extremities—that is, at the corners of the eyes. (5) They interlace. "Dalitam" means blossomed. "Kandoṭṭaṃ" means the blue lotus. [Kāmandakī] "Mohanaṃ" means sexual union.

[2] *Īṣat*: slightly; *nyastaṃ*: cast down; *valitena*: with a rolling motion; *viṣamaṃ*: unevenly, so as to be mutually unbearable. (6) *Kuñcitaprāntaṃ*: with the corners of the eyes contracted. *Premodbhedena*: by the emergence of affection; *stimitaṃ*: motionless; and *lulitaṃ*: agitated. *Ākuñcite bhruvau yatra*: where the eyebrows are arched. *Antar* means "within," i.e., in the heart. *Modaḥ*: joy. *Masṛṇaṃ* is an adverbial modifier.

That in which their eyes are *ākekarā*—having squinting corners due to the *vibhāvas* such as shame and passion arising from seeing one another—is what has been "seen": the act of looking. This clearly proclaims that these two repeatedly experience a delusion of the mind. (8) "The *ākekarā* glance is remembered as having contracted corners, being joyful, half-closed, and with the pupil frequently rolling back. Its application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: "The *ākekarā* [glance] is used when something is difficult to see, and also for a look made during separation. (00)

(9) Therein, by the slight oblique turning and unevenness [of the eyes], and by the corners being narrowed, the "curved outer corners" (*ākuñcitapuṭāpāṅga*) is shown. By the phrase "stilled and stirred by the breaking forth of love," it is said that the pupils repeatedly turn back. The slight contraction of the eyebrows constitutes the body of the *ākekara* [glance]. And by the third quarter-verse, the meaning of the second quarter-verse is established.
(10) [2] MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend Buddharakṣitā, will this lotus-eyed one, the giver of my life, be seen once again?

Buddharakṣitā: If fate should be favorable. [Mādhava: [3] This thread, consisting of the hope for the attainment of Mālatī, which has served as the support for my heart’s consolation until now—let it be severed now. Let this fragile state of longing, which is itself on the verge of breaking, let this mental anguish (ādhi)—this disease of the mind—spread without restraint. And let the bond of fickleness establish its true footing in me. Through the fulfillment of my desire, may the Creator be free from anxiety.

And let the Mind-born (the God of Love), who inflicts unbearable pain without Mālatī, have accomplished his purpose. [3] [4] "Its being difficult to obtain" is due to its dependence on another. "Pariṇatiḥ" means the final conclusion. Her face has its luster fading away; for this very reason, it possesses the brilliance of the morning moon. [Makaranda: "Cessation" (*virata*) means having desisted. "It moistens" (*dravayati*) means it brings about a state of softness or tenderness. Regarding the renunciation (*pravrajyā*) characterized by the cessation of all worldly desires preceded by the taking of vows, there is a specific practice (*samudācāra*)—concerning meditation, concentration, and so forth—which is easily obtained (*sulabha*), meaning inevitable, and which has come down through tradition (*saṃpradāyāgata*). Your effort, which is averse to that [practice], is for the time being "uninterrupted" (*prasakta*), meaning free from interruption. And this much alone constitutes the visible collection of causal factors (*dṛṣṭasāmagrī*) in this encounter.

Even if that [effort] were present, if the failure to accomplish the task were due solely to a deficiency in unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*), then that would not be dependent on anyone. For this very reason they say: "If it is not accomplished despite effort having been made, what fault is there in this?

[7] Mālatī: O noble one, you who bring delight to my eyes, this is the last time you shall be seen. Lavaṅgikā: Alas, woe! Woe! My dear friend has been placed in mortal danger by the minister.

Mālatī: Now the fruit of my thirst for life has ripened. And the Kāpālika nature of my father has been fully realized through his cruelty. The terrible conclusion, befitting the machinations of cursed fate, has arrived. To whom shall I, of such wretched fortune, offer reproach? Or whom, being without refuge, shall I take as my protector?

The lamentation for the preservation of life is as follows: "Now the fruit has ripened" of that life which, during the state of experiencing the most intense pain of separation, was resolved upon abandoning, yet was sustained by various cooling treatments and the sight of Madhava’s likeness and other such things. "Kāpālikatva" means cruelty.

This also indicates the resolve of Aghoraghaṇṭa, just as there was the speech of Daśaratha’s son toward Sītā when he was intent on slaying the golden deer Mārīca: "May this variegated tunic take you away at once! [Sītā: "O forest deity, may this evil be averted! May not Karbuṛa seize her. (12)

[Mādhava: The fulfillment of his birth: the bliss of contentment produced by the attainment of Mālatī. (13) The indication of future events is something other than the sale of human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*). In the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata*, within the cycle of the cremation ground (*śmaśāna-saṃsāra*), there is a method consisting solely of an act of extreme audacity: taking human flesh from the hands of heroes and granting a desired boon to a hero.
